Introdiiction Previous palaeomagnetic studies have shown that the palaeolatitude of south-east Australia was high (70"-80" for Canberra) from the Late Carboniferous to the Middle Cretaceous (Irving, Robertson & Stott 1963; Irving 1966). To compare the land-based polar changes with the ocean-floor drift south of Australia requires that a series of poles from well-dated rocks be determined with considerable accuracy (polar errors of 5" or less). Previous palaeomagnetic measurements are generally inadequate for this purpose, either because the age of the rocks was not known precisely or because large polar errors resulted from sampling at only a few localities. Twenty sites in the Older Volcanics of Victoria have been studies by Mumme (1963) following a preliminary investigation by Green & Irving (1958). On palaeonto- logical grounds these basalts are thought to be Palaeoceilto Eocene in age (Cookson & Dettman 1959; Singleton & Joyce 1969). Irving, Stott &Ward (1961) investigated eight sites from the Tertiary basalts of.New South Wales. The localities sampled are now known to range in age from about 15 to 45 m.yr (McDougall & Wilkinson 1967; Stipp & McDougall 1968; and other unpublished information). Volcanics in southern Queensland have been studied at 11 sites by Robertson (1966). Webb, Stevens & McDougall (1967) report the age of these rocks as ranging from 25 to 21 m.yr. The Newer Volcanics of Victoria have been investigated by Green & Irving (1958), Parry (1960) and McDo

(1966). These latter authors found their K-Ar age ranged from 5 to 05m.yr, and other evidence indicates activity until about 5000 years ago. A considerable number of Cenozoic shield volcanoes occur near the eastern margin of Australia and these provide suitable sequences of lava flows both for detailed palaeomagnetic work and K-Ar dating. In this paper combined palaeo- magnetic and dating measurements are reported from three large shield volcanoes in northern New South Wales. These are the Nandewar, Liverpool and Barrington Volcanoes (Fig. 1). Their numerous thin flows are relatively well exposed, allowing systematic collections of samples to be made. By working on thick sequences of lava flows the internal consistency of K-Ar dates is checked, and a reliable age can be found. The palaeomagnetic data also provides information on the frequency of reversals of the geomagnetic field at various times during the Cenozoic. This infor- mation can then be compared with the geomagnetic polarity time scale deduced for the Cenozoic from sea-floor spreading measurements (Heirtzler et al. 1968). 2. Remanent Magnetization Two cylindrical specimens (2.5 cm in diameter, 2.2 cm long) from each drill core were used for remanence measurement and partial demagne- tization in alternating magnetic fields (AF) of up to 800 Oe. The latter was done to remove recently acquired, low stability components of remanent magnetization, with the objective to isolate original remanent magnetization acquired during cooling (thermoremanent magnetization, TRM) and/or possibly shortly thereafter by oxidation of original titanomagnetite or produc- tion of secondary magnetite during serpentiniza- tion (chemical remanent magnetization, CRM). This original remanent magnetization is expec- ted to show good stability; that is, sufficiently high coercive force. A third specimen from 40 cores was thermally demagnetized. The magnetization direction of each core was required to show reasonable homogeneity during AF demagnetization. Lack (Received 1970 February 2) Summary The magnetization of samples from 29 sites in Lower Cambrian Volcanics and interbedded sediments, collected over an area of 250000km2 of northern Australia, has been investigated. Fourteen of the sites respond to magnetic cleaning, although in one case thermal cleaning is preferred. The small departure from the present south geographic pole is in the correct sense required by sea-floor spreading south of Australia. Introduction The Pre-Cambrian Giles Complex is a series of layered mafic and ultramafic intrusions extending over an area of at least 12000 sq km of Central Australia (Fig. 1). Nesbitt & Talbot (1966) have described the Complex. In addition to palaeo- magnetic studies, it was expected that investigation of the magnetic properties of the rocks could provide information on the structural relationships (and history) of the Complex. Complementing magnetic studies, this investigation included study of certain petrological/mineralogical properties of these coarse-grained rocks. Present weathering of the Giles Complex rocks is characteristic of arid regions, although chemical weathering has emphasized the strongly developed layering of the intrusions. The mafic portions tend only to have thin weathering rinds (at times less than a millimetre in thickness). Introduction This note describes first results from a palaeomag- netic research program designed to investigate the Lower Palaeozoic geomagnetic field and the relation of the major crustal blocks in Australia. Recent inter- pretation [ 1, 2] of the geological history of southeast Australia, in terms of plate tectonics, have stressed the complex tectonic history the region suffered dur- ing the Lower Palaeozoic. Therefore, to successfully describe an apparent polar wander path for Australia for this period, it would seem that results may be bet- ter obtained from localities situated in the older crustal regions. Indeed, almost all Lower Palaeozoic investiga- tions have been carried out with material sampled from the Northern Territory and South Australia, viz. Cambrian [3, 6] and Ordovician [7]. If agreement be- tween the palaeomagnetic records for the Lower Pa- laeozoic from separate crustal regions within Austra- fia can be demonstrated, then the relationship of Australia to the rest of Gondwanaland may be clarified. EMBLETON (With 1 Table and 3 Figures) (MS received 18 February 1974; revised MS received 25 June 1974) ABSTRACT Palaeomagnetic results from 40 dykes sampled on Eyre Peninsula and Yorke Peninsula, South Australia, are inconsistent with the clockwise rotation of the 'foot' of Yorke Peninsula by fault-drag during the Early Ordovician. A reinter- pretation of earlier data from Tasmania also indicates that the east-west structural trends in the Mount Reed volcanic arc and Dundas Trough are primary.

sistent with the clockwise rotation of the 'foot' of Yorke Peninsula by fault-drag during the Early Ordovician. A reinter- pretation of earlier data from Tasmania also indicates that the east-west structural trends in the Mount Reed volcanic arc and Dundas Trough are primary. The effects of shearing were probably restricted to linear displacements without causing rotation of adjacent structural elements. Late Precambrian and Cambrian palaeo- magnetic data from Fleurieu Peninsula and Kangaroo Island have also been analysed. They do not clarify the pattern of structural evolution in the southern part of the Adelaide Orogen because the magnetic remanence was probably acquired syntectonically. They regarded the southern part of the Adelaide Orogen as having been bent in a westerly direction by large-scale fault-drag along this shear. suggested two possible explanations for the discrepancy. (1) Coalification results from temperatures maintained for tens of millions of years, whereas remagnetization might have resulted from a shorter pulse of higher temperature, or (2) multidomain grains, which were detected in the Milton Monzonite, might have different time-temperature relations than single-domain grains. It is important to settle this question because the remagnetization temperature approach to basin analysis is quick, inexpensive, and much more widely applicable than vitrinite reflectance or other measures of organic diagenesis. Other, independent studies on sandstones and limestones in the Hercynian and Appalachian orogens of Europe and North America [Chama- laun, 1964; Kent, 1985] have also yielded unblocking tempera- tures that are \"anomalously high\" (i.e., implying unrealistically high regional T values). Thus the remagnetization problem is not limited to a particular lithology, depositional-erosional history, or tectonic setting, and its solution is likely to lie in some general magnetic phenomenon. With this background in mind, we restudied the Milton Monzonite with a greater areal coverage of sites and more comprehensive thermal treatments than in Schmidt and Embleton's [1981] study.

Two advantages of this method of removing secondary com- ponents, compared with standard thermal and magnetic clean- ing, deserve mention. First, it is possible, by using our iterative method, to remove a secondary component with a higher coercivity (impossible with magnetic cleaning) or a higher blocking temperature (impossible with thermal cleaning) than that of the primary component with which it is physically associated, as long as the secondary direction is known. This procedure is advantageous in partly weathered rocks, com- monly oxidized, in which the weathered material is likely to be hematite, with a higher coercivity and blocking temperature than the primary component (if magnetite). Second, if a secondary component is suspected, different possible directions for it, related to the time of formation as deduced from geological reasoning, may be tested against each other for minimum dispersion. (Australia) (Submitted September 15, 1975; revised version accepted February 3, 1976) ABSTRACT Schmidt, P.W., 1976. A new palaeomagnetic investigation of Mesozoic igneous rocks in Australia. Tectonophysics, 33: l-13. Palaeomagnetic results have been obtained from four Australian igneous rock forma- tions ranging in age from Early Jurassic to Early Cretaceous. These new sampling locali- ties cover a much larger area than previously represented by Australian data. It is demon- strated that the pole positions yielded by the Kangaroo Island basalt (viz. 39”s 183” E, Ags = 11”) dated at 170 m.y. and the Early Jurassic western Victoria basalts (viz. 47”s 186” E, A95 = 4” ) agree with results from other continents in the context of Gondwana- land. The pole position for the Bendigo dykes (47” S 135’E, Ags = 39” ) confirm the ‘anomalous’ results previously obtained from southeastern Australia. The fourth pole po- sition, obtained from the Bunbury basalt of Western Australia (dated at around 90 m.y.) is in good agreement with other Cretaceous data for Australia, implying that pole posi- tions for the Jurrassic and Cretaceous periods should now be considered separately. INTRODUCTION Several Australian Mesozoic rock bodies received palaeomagnetic atten- tion over a decade ago (Almond et al., 1956; Irving, 1956 and 1963; Boesen et al., 1961; Robertson and Hastie, 1962; Robertson, 1963; and Stott, 1963), however no further investigations have been reported since. These rock types embrace sedimentary and igneous units which lie within the southern por- tion of the Tasman erogenic zone re

e simi- lar in age (McDougall, 1963) and closely related chemically (Compston et al., 1968), their respective pole positions remain quite distinct after rotation of Australia and Antarctica to their pre-drift positions as predicted by geo- metrical and geological constraints (Sproll and Dietz, 1969; and Smith and Hallam, 1970). Griffith (1971) has suggested relative motion of Tasmania prior to the in- trusion of the Tasm~ian dolerites as an explanation. On the other hand Francheteau (1970) considers the results of the Fenar dolerites to be at fault. These explanations are unsatisfactory. Firstly, results from serveral Mesozoic rock-formations from mainland Australia are in good agreement with the re- sults from Tasmania (Irving et al., 1963) and consequently any motion rela- tive to Antarctica at that time would presumably also have involved this por- tion of the mainland. Results from leg 27 of the Deep Sea Drilling Project (DSDP) do not clarify the Mesozoic problem. Mesozoic basalts from bore- cores off the northwest shelf yield a pole locus consistent with the south- eastern Australian data whereas bore-core material drilled off the Perth shelf yields a pole locus consistent with the Ferrar dolerite pole of Antarctica (McElhinny, 1974; McElhinny and Embleton, 1974). These new sampling locali- ties cover a much larger area than previously represented by Australian data. It is demon- strated that the pole positions yielded by the Kangaroo Island basalt (viz. 39”s 183” E, Ags = 11”) dated at 170 m.y. and the Early Jurassic western Victoria basalts (viz. 47”s 186” E, A95 = 4” ) agree with results from other continents in the context of Gondwana- land. Tectonophysics, 33: l-13. Palaeomagnetic results have been obtained from four Australian igneous rock forma- tions ranging in age from Early Jurassic to Early Cretaceous. These new sampling locali- ties cover a much larger area than previously represented by Australian data. It is demon- strated that the pole positions yielded by the Kangaroo Island basalt (viz. 39”s 183” E, Ags = 11”) dated at 170 m.y. and the Early Jurassic western Victoria basalts (viz. 47”s 186” E, A95 = 4” ) agree with results from other continents in the context of Gondwana- land. The pole position for the Bendigo dykes (47” S 135’E, Ags = 39” ) confirm the ‘anomalous’ results previously obtained from southeastern Australia. The fourth pole po- sition, obtained from the Bunbury basalt of Western Australia (dated at around 90 m.y.) is in good agreement with other Cretaceous data for Australia, implying that pole posi- tions for the Jurrassic and Cretaceous periods should now be considered separately. INTRODUCTION Several Australian Mesozoic rock bodies received palaeomagnetic atten- tion over a decade ago (Almond et al., 1956; Irving, 1956 and 1963; Boesen et al., 1961; Robertson and Hastie, 1962; Robertson, 1963; and Stott, 1963), however no further investigations have been reported since. These rock types embrace sedimentary and igneous units which lie within the southern por- tion of the Tasman erogenic zone re

e simi- lar in age (McDougall, 1963) and closely related chemically (Compston et al., 1968), their respective pole positions remain quite distinct after rotation of Australia and Antarctica to their pre-drift positions as predicted by geo- metrical and geological constraints (Sproll and Dietz, 1969; and Smith and Hallam, 1970). Griffith (1971) has suggested relative motion of Tasmania prior to the in- trusion of the Tasm~ian dolerites as an explanation. On the other hand Francheteau (1970) considers the results of the Fenar dolerites to be at fault. These explanations are unsatisfactory. Firstly, results from serveral Mesozoic rock-formations from mainland Australia are in good agreement with the re- sults from Tasmania (Irving et al., 1963) and consequently any motion rela- tive to Antarctica at that time would presumably also have involved this por- tion of the mainland. Results from leg 27 of the Deep Sea Drilling Project (DSDP) do not clarify the Mesozoic problem. Mesozoic basalts from bore- cores off the northwest shelf yield a pole locus consistent with the south- eastern Australian data whereas bore-core material drilled off the Perth shelf yields a pole locus consistent with the Ferrar dolerite pole of Antarctica (McElhinny, 1974; McElhinny and Embleton, 1974). Firstly, results from serveral Mesozoic rock-formations from mainland Australia are in good agreement with the re- sults from Tasmania (Irving et al., 1963) and consequently any motion rela- tive to Antarctica at that time would presumably also have involved this por- tion of the mainland. Results from leg 27 of the Deep Sea Drilling Project (DSDP) do not clarify the Mesozoic problem. Mesozoic basalts from bore- cores off the northwest shelf yield a pole locus consistent with the south- eastern Australian data whereas bore-core material drilled off the Perth shelf yields a pole locus consistent with the Ferrar dolerite pole of Antarctica (McElhinny, 1974; McElhinny and Embleton, 1974). Precambrian Res., 3: 231--241. A routine palaeomagnetic study of the 1800 Ma old Hart dolerite shows that sample directions of magnetism give good within-site grouping at 12 sites after magnetic cleaning. However, the site mean directions are scattered over one-quarter of the sphere, a feature that apparently does not arise from poor structural control. A baked contact test confirms that the magnetization is original. Comparison of bulk NRM, TRM, ARM and saturation IRM properties has been made with the Modipe gabbro of southern Africa from which a palaeointensity has previously been estimated. These measurements are consistent with the hypothesis that the main dipole field intensity temporarily was much reduced with respect to the non-dipole field 1800 m.y. ago resulting in increased directional scatter from secular variation. The average of the site VGPs at 29N 46E with Ags = 24 ° thus is still a viable estimate of the palaeomagnetic pole at that time bearing in mind the larger than usual statistical error associated with it. (1965) who describe it as the most extensively developed Pre- cambrian dolerite known, the total area of outcrop being of the same order as that of the Tasmanian dolerite. It consists of a series of anastomosing sills with associated granophyres, the thickness of individual sills ranging from 20 to 2000 m, the largest intruding the dominantly arenaceous Speewah Group. J. J. Embleton ABSTRACT. The thermal stability of the magnetism in specimens from fourteen oriented core samples of red-beds belonging to the Mulga Downs Group was satisfactorily tested using the progressive partial thermal demagnetization technique up to 620°C. Magnetic remanence considered primary and acquired at the time of rock formation was isolated in twenty-one specimens from twelve samples: they yield a palaeomagnetic pole situated at 54°S, 96°E (A95 = 11°). This supports an earlier result obtained from the Middle Devonian Housetop Granite of Tasmania but differs substantially from results obtained from the Lochiel Formation of southeastern New South Wales. The result from the Mulga Downs Group is interpreted as emphasizing the discrepancy between the Palaeozoic palaeomagnetic results from the main Australian platform, and those from the Lachlan Fold Belt. A geologic map of the area having the best exposure, Ross River, is shown in Fig. 2. This area is on the north limb of an east-west-trending syncline, and samples were ob- tained from strata exposed by the Ross River. The strata dip uniformly between 36 ° and 37 ° to the south, with no other structural complications. Similar sections are exposed at the other three localities, Valley Dam, Aeryonga Gorge, and Central Mt. Stewart, although structural attitudes are different. The fold test of Graham [5] offers a second check on the time of acquisition of the magnetiza- tion in the Amadeus Basin. However, before it can be applied to the sequence, it is necessary to deter- mine whether significant amounts of apparent polar wander have occurred in the time interval covered, which, as noted previously, may be as long as 96 m.y. Results for the primary magnetic components have therefore been split into three groups based on the stratigraphy. These groups are (1) the Pertatataka Formation and the basal part of the Arumbera Sandstone, (2) the remainder of the Arumbera Sandstone, and (3) the Box Hole, Allua, Eninta and Todd River Dolomite Formations. The directions for each of these groups shown in Fig. 6 overlap at the 95% level showing that there was insignificant apparent polar wander during this time, and imply- ing that all of the data may legitimately be com- bined for the fold test. Paleomagnetic samples in that study were collected at about 1-m intervals from an 800 m thick sedimen- tary sequence that crosses the Precambrian-Cambrian boundary. A large difference in magnetic reversal frequency across the sequence is revealed by thermal demagnetization. The lower 500 m contains two magnetozones whose contact is marked by a polarity transition that lies in the lower member of the Arumbera Sandstone. The upper 300 m of section are characterized by mixed polarities with, as yet, an incompletely determined number of magneto- zones. Paleomagnetic tests presented in this paper suggest that one component of the stable magnetiza- tion was acquired in a geologically short time after deposition, and that this magnetization therefore is equivalent in age to the fossils in the sequence. INTRODUCTION The Tasmanian Dolerites occur as large intrusive sheets, commonly exceeding 300 m in thickness, and dyke-like bodies emplaced in nearly flat-lying Permian and Triassic sedi- mentary rocks; they crop out over an area of some 15 000 km2 mainly in the eastern half of Tasmania (Fig. 1). The K-Ar ages on this intrusive body ranged from 140 to 170 m.y. based upon measurements on total-rock samples, plagioclase, anorthoclase, and clino- pyroxene. INTRODUCTION The theory of plate tectonics has successfully combined palaeomagnetically determined polarwander curves and marine geophysical data into a coherent description of continental motions during the Phanerozoic (McElhinny, 1973). Extrapolation of these concepts to the Precambrian is of considerable interest for an understanding of the development of intra- cratonic mobile belts and the general tectonic regime prevailing during earliest history of the Earth's crust (Rutland, 1973; Sutton & Watson, 1974; Smith, 1976; McElhinny & McWilliams, 1977). Comparison of palaeo- magnetically-determined polarwander curves from different cratons within the same con- tinent may reveal the extent and timing of relative motions between cratons. At the same time polarwander curves may be used as a magnetostratigraphical tool to determine the age or relative stratigraphical position of for- mations that cannot otherwise be dated. eomag- netic result for the Gawler Craton, South Aus- tralia, based on the very precisely dated Gawler Range Volcanics (Compston & Arriens, 1968; Webb, 1976). Comparison with results obtained previously (Chamalaun & Porath, 1968; Giddings & Embleton, 1976), suggests that the pole corresponding to 1500 m.y. is now well established for the Gawler Craton. With regard to the overall Australian Precambrian polarwander curve of McElhinny & Embleton (1976), the Gawler Craton data suggest only a minor modification in the age labelling. Furthermore, the results have placed a firm age on the final stages of the ore forma- tion of the Middleback Ranges hematite ore bodies, and appear to favour a hypogene origin for the ore. GEOLOGICAL SETTING The Gawler Range Volcanics occur in the northern part of Eyre Peninsula in South Aus- tralia (see Fig. 1) and form the most extensive mass of calc-alkaline igneous rocks in Aus- tralia. Known outcrops cover some 25 000 km2 but it is suspected that originally a much larger area may have been covered (Blissett, 1975). First discovered by Brown in 1885, the volcanics received little attention until Craw- ford (1963) published a description of large arc-like structures and Turner (1975) provided a detailed petrological account of the area near Uno. In 1972 the Sou

oro- geny commenced with the extrusion of the Gawler Range Volcanics, and terminated with the extrusion of postorogenic granites c. 1600- 1450 m.y. This Jast plutonic event marked the final phase of cratonization of the Gawler Craton. Discussing the tectonic evolution of the Gawler Craton, Rutland (1973), and Glen et al. (1977), suggested that the craton was at a relatively high crustal level at the time of formation of the Gawler Range Volcanics and that its evolution may represent a Pre- cambrian variant of a Cordilleran orogeny with subduction from the east. The Middleback Group contains banded iron formations which are host rocks to the hematite ore bodies, and for which a correlation with the Mt Bruce Supergroup in the Hamersley Ranges of Western Australia has been suggested (Thom- son, 1976). The geomagnetic field and secular variation The geomagnetic field is produced by a dynamo process that operates within the fluid core of the Earth (Malkus 1968). Using spherical harmonic analysis the magnetic field is separated into a dipole component and a non-dipole component. The latter is obtained by subtracting the field corresponding to the dipole from the total magnetic field (Bullard et al. 1950). The dipole is best represented at present by a dipole inclined at 11.4" to the rotation axis of the Earth in the meridional plane of longitude 69.8" W (Doell & Cox 1971). Observati

The precession of the dipole around the rotation axis (the dipole wobble) provides an important contribution to the PSV. The period of the precession is still very poorly known but is probably in the order of lo4 to lo5 years (Cox & Doell 1964; Doell & Cox 1965). Three weathered samples from Site A3, at Peppermint Bay about eight miles east of Cygnet, were measured to test the effect of weathering. Two samples from Site B6, a syenite-porphyry dyke on the foreshore gave random directions (R = 2.4, N = 6). Three samples from site C1, in the hybrid zone, were taken from a contact between syenite-pegmatite and altered dolerite. Six specimens from the syenite and the dolerite side of the contact, and also from the contact itself, were measured. A paleomagnetic study has been made of a succession of 139 non- overlapping basaltic lavas, representing 91 per cent of the longest remaining succession of flows associated with the Paleogene Mull volcano. All the lavas have experienced considerable hydrothermal alteration, probably at up to several million years after initial magnetization and frequently with alteration to the opaque minerals and the production of new potentially magnetic phases. The question of whether directional remagnetization has taken place while preserving within-unit directional consistency and discreteness of unit mean direction is discussed. A magnetic polarity sequence has been developed for the Late Cretaceous from about 500 stratigraphic samples of the Scaglia Rossa lime- stone from a 250-m thick section near Cubbio, Italy. Although a large soft component is present in all samples, it is possible to remove it by alternating field magnetic cleaning. fully as a correlation tool, together with palaeontological zonation for the dating of modern unconsolidated deep sea sediments (Hays & Opdyke 1967). Indurated pelagic limestones have similar advantages for magnetic stratigraphy analysis; they represent essentially con- tinuous sedimentation and contain abundant datable fossils. Although their magnetization is extremely weak, it can be readily measured with modern computer-controlled spinner magnetometers or cryogenic magnetometers. Previous work on the pelagic Scaglia Rossa limestone from a number of sites distributed throughout Umbria, Italy, gave consistent palaeomagnetic results (Lowrie & Alvarez 1974, 1975; Channel1 & Tarling 1975; VandenBerg, Klootwijk & Wonders 1977). In a pilot magnetic stratigraphy study of an essentially complete single exposure near Gubbio, ranging from Turonian to Eocene in age, 16 stratigraphically spaced sites were sampled (Alvarez & Lowrie 1974; Lowrie & Alvarez 1975). Many of these sites were reversely magnetized. The limestone possessed satisfactory magnetic properties and its sedimentology and palaeonto- logy were known. The East Gargano Basin (Fig. 1) developed within the Apulian platform carbonates during the Late Jurassic and Early Cretaceous. Fine-grained pelagic limestones were deposited in this basin throughout the Cretaceous and Early Tertiary. Introduction The Southern Apennines represent part of the deformed Periadriatic continental margin (D'Argenio 1974) which can be subdivided into a number of structural-stratigraphic units (D'Argenio & Scandone 1970; D'Argenio, Pescatore & Scandone 1975 ; Ippolito et al. 1975; Catalan0 et ul. 1977). Palaeomagnetic results obtained from a 7-m sedimentary sequence in southern British Columbia spanning approximately 9000 yr (- 22 000 to - 3 1 000 yr BP based on radiocarbon dates) are reported and analysed. Remanence directions from 37 horizons spread throughout the section have been determined, and no evidence of the geomagnetic excursion observed at Lake Mungo, Australia (- 31 000-28 000 yr BP), or that observed at Mono Lake, California (25 000-24 000 yr BP) is present. However, regular oscil- lations in the remanence vectors are observed, and maximum entropy spectral analysis, after mapping the remanence directions on to the complex plane, reveals peaks at periods of approximately 2000 and 5000yr. The 2000-yr peak is associated with clockwise looping of the geomagnetic vector, and therefore most likely represents the time associated with one full cycle of the westward drift of the non-dipole field. The 5000-yr peak is associated with elliptical counterclockwise looping of the local geomagnetic vector and may be indicative of counterclockwise motion of the geomagnetic dipole axis. The 5000-yr peak is associated with elliptical counterclockwise looping of the local geomagnetic vector and may be indicative of counterclockwise motion of the geomagnetic dipole axis. Introduction Since the beginning of the study of magnetization in recent sediments, interesting periodici- ties in the behaviour of the geomagnetic field have been noticed (Johnson, Murphy & Torreson 1948; Nagata, Hirao & Yoshikawa 1949; Mackereth 1971; Creer 1974; Creer, Gross & Lineback 1976; Opdyke er al. 1972). It has, in fact, become generally accepted that the study of these periodicities is critical to the understanding of the physical mecha- nisms underlying geomagnetic secular variation. Variations in declination and inclination have been examined in detail by many authors, but unfortunately in most cases the two directional elements have not been studied simultaneously. Where it has been possible to examine the two-dimensional oscillatory behaviour of palaeomagnetic directions, a strong tendency towards looping has often been observed (Denham 1974) as in the case of the well-known London and Paris historical records. cated methods of spectral analysis is desirable. Denham (1975) outlines the particular method of spectral analysis best suited to palaeomagnetic data. The method involves map- ping the data on to the complex plane about the appropriate norm, and then analysing the resulting complex time series by means of the so-called maximum entropy method of spec- tral analysis. The use of Burg's (1967, 1968) maximum entropy spectral estimator was suggested because of its obvious superiority over other techniques in dealing with short, relatively noisy data sets. The advantage of the complex representation of the data is that all the directional information is contained in a single time series. As a result, one can determine not only the power at a given frequency, but also the tendemy towards clockwise or counterclockwise looping at that frequency. In this paper palaeomagnetic data recently obtained from a sedimentary sequence in southern British Columbia are presented which constitute a time series of ancient geomag- netic directions spanning approximately 9000 yr. Samples from the Nexg Sandstone of the Lower Cambrian- Precambrian boundary in South Bomholm reveal a stable NRM with a direc- tion after magnetic cleaning of D = 226", I = - 30" (ag5 = 11 So). This NRM appears to originate in the detrital hematite grains rather than in the red cement of the sandstone. The stable NRM is likely to be of primary origin and reflects a Lower Cambrian pole at 104" W, 38" N (dp = 7", dm = 1 lo). Apparent discrepancies between the Bornholm pole and the few other published Early Cambrian/Late Precambrian poles from the Baltic Shield are consistent with the suggestion of large polar movements in those times. 1 Introduction Deviating Lower Palaeozoic poles have been reported for the Cambrian (Briden, Irons & Johnson 1971 ; Poorter 1972a; Storetvedt 1973; Tarling 1974) as well as for the Ordovician rocks (Creer 1970; Briden, Morris & Piper 1973; Piper 19

eozoic, but Storetvedt (1973) attributes the deviating results to false palaeomagnetic directions 'resulting from oversimplified analysis of complex magnetic components', and he continues to believe that the Lower Palaeozoic pole was apparently fixed for at least 300 Myr. A well-defined Lower Cambrian palaeomagnetic polar path is of great importance, fustly for continuation of the polar curve from the Early Palaeozoic to the Late Precambrian times, and secondly for a study of the polar pattern at around the time of the Eocambrian glacia- tion. For this study the samples were collected from the Nexb sandstone of Borriholm because this hematite-bearing rock promised to be usable for palaeomagnetic investigation. It is concluded that the rocks were laid down in late Permian time just before the close of the reversed Kiaman geomagnetic epoch. Subsequent oxidation and partial remagnetization basic- ally occurred in late Permian-Triassic time, during a period characterized by alternating field polarity. The northerly directional trends are more pronounced in the strongly oxidized specimens, i.e. those with a high haematite content, and therefore the NNW direction is likely to represent a field component impressed through remagnetization rather than being a result of partial self-reversal. The result suggests that the dominant remagnetization processes occurred in roughly the same dipole field in which the original magnetization was acquired. The primary tectonic situation and the lengthy magnetization history (impressing time-average palaeomagnetic vectors even in single speci- mens) suggest that the available data may serve as an adequate basis for palaeomagnetic and tectonic conclusions for Sardinia. The distribution of collected sites is shown in Fig. 1. The sampled material which embraces rhyolitic tuffs and a few ignimbritic lavas varies in colour from dark grey to pinkish. The formation sits approxi- mately horizontal (Traversa 1966) and the local structural situation appears to be original. Therefore, no tectonic corrections have been applied for the investigated sites. On average, seven specimens from each site have been subjected to stepwise thermal demagnetization up to a maximum of 650°C in a residual magnetic field of about 5 y. For remanence measurements an astatic magnetometer as well as commercial spinner magneto- meters have been used after each heating step. Vector subtraction analysis (cf: e.g. Roy & Park 1974) has been carried out on all speci- mens defining directional paths on progressive demagnetization. By this technique one can determine the direction of an erased vector provided that there is a range of demagnetization for which only this one component is being removed. A wide range of Late Ordovician-Lower Silurian (Llandovery) intrusions yield directions of magnetization unlike any previously identified from Lower Palaeozoic rocks of Britain, but highly stable to thermal and af demagnetiza- tion, and include a reversal of magnetization. The collective results define a large movement relative to the dipole axis over a period of less than 10 Ma between c.445 and 425 Ma; part of this movement can be explained in terms of complex rotations of the British region during late Ordovician and early Silurian tectonism within the

The polarity sequence at 60 % 2 Ma is then R + N + R with the plateau lavas during the first reversed period, the later part of the centre and the E-W dykes during the normal period and NW-SE regional dykes throughout. Thus the Basal Member and Member A are somewhat older than we previously believed, but age assignments for major fossil localities are un- affected. The inferred age ranges for the Shungura and Usno Formations are 3.5 to 0.8 Myr and 3.7 to 2.8 Myr respectively. The present analysis yields five zones of normal polarity in the lower Matuyama Reversed Epoch, that is, between the MatuyamalCauss transition and the base of the Olduvai. All were found both in the previous data and in the new samples taken at different locations. For three of the five zones an unbroken series of normal samples extends over several lithologies, so a geomagnetic event is indicated. These forma- tions have received intensive geological and palaeontological study over the past decade (Coppens et al. 1976).
